title: Looking beyond the baseline: how scenario synthesis helps assess risks
author: European Central Bank
text:
THE ECB BLOGLooking beyond the baseline: how scenario synthesis helps assess risks24 November 2026By Marta Bańbura, Domenico Giannone, Filippo Durero, Yiqiao Sun and Srečko ZimicScenario analysis is an increasingly important tool for monetary policy. This blog shows how scenario synthesis links narrative scenarios with probabilistic risk assessments, helping policymakers evaluate scenario relevance, coverage and shifts in risk perceptions as new information arrives.Why are scenarios needed?When the ECB’s Governing Council makes monetary policy decisions, it does not focus solely on the most likely forecast for inflation and growth. It must also assess the risks and uncertainty surrounding that outlook.To do so, the ECB uses a range of methods and tools, including statistical risk measures based on past forecast errors or model output, an internal survey of staff views on risks known as the quantitative risk assessment (QRA) and sensitivity and scenario analysis. No single approach captures every aspect of uncertainty – each offers a different perspective on the risks facing the economy.[1] See Ciccarelli, M., Darracq Pariès, P., Landau, B. and Sousa, J. (2025), “Exploring an uncertain future with the help of scenarios”, The ECB Blog, ECB, 15 January and Workstream 1: Changing economic and inflation environment (2025), “A strategic view on the economic and inflation environment in the euro area”, Occasional Paper Series, No 371, ECB, June. Scenario analysis complements the statistical risk measures in two important ways. First, it provides narratives. Scenarios explore specific risk events such as an energy shock, a geopolitical escalation, a trade disruption or tighter financial conditions, illustrating the economic channels through which they could affect inflation and growth.Second, scenarios help policymakers examine developments that have little or no precedent. This is particularly important during periods of structural change or heightened geopolitical stress because risk measures based mainly on past events and data may understate the risks involved and the range of possible outcomes. A clear example of this is the energy crisis following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The statistical measure of risks (illustrated in Chart 1 by a dark blue line) around the baseline Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) inflation forecast of 5.1% year-on-year, which was built on historical model residuals, did not capture the actual inflation outcome of 8.4% year-on-year. By contrast, the adverse and severe scenarios, respectively concentrated around 5.9% and 7.1%, highlighted risks that historical residuals alone would have missed. The scenarios helped broaden the range of possibilities considered in the policymaking process and brought the risk assessment closer to what ultimately occurred. Chart 1Risks to baseline HICP inflation for 2022 (y-axis: value of probability density function; x-axis: annual percentage change)Sources: ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area, March 2022 and ECB staff calculations.Notes: The chart illustrates how alternative scenarios can cover a wider range of inflation outcomes than baseline uncertainty. Baseline uncertainty is captured by a probability distribution derived from historical ECB-BASE model residuals. Scenario synthesis: linking narratives and risk measuresA scenario describes what could happen if a particular risk materialises. Once several scenarios are available, two questions arise: first, how relevant is each scenario and, second, how well do they collectively capture the overall risks? To answer these questions, we need to link these scenarios to some overall and forward-looking reference measures of risk. Such measures may come from the ECB/Eurosystem’s QRA, options-implied probability distributions from financial markets or probability assessments from professional forecasters.[2] The risk measures referred to in this blog are formally probability distributions, and the two terms are used interchangeably. These measures show how markets, forecasters or policymakers see the balance of risks. However, they do not come with an underlying narrative; nor do they explain the relative importance of individual risk events or why risk perceptions are shifting.Scenario synthesis provides that missing link.[3] See Adrian, T., Giannone, D., Luciani, M. and West, M. (2025), “Scenario Synthesis and Macroeconomic Risk”, Finance and Economics Discussion Series, No 2025-36, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Washington, May and Adrian, T., Giannone, D., Luciani, M. and West, M. (2026), “Risks and Uncertainty in Monetary Policy”, 2606.16708v1, 26 June. It combines the baseline outlook with a set of alternative scenarios in a way that best matches one of these overall reference risk measures. In practice, this means deriving a synthetic distribution by assigning a weight to each scenario which reflects the degree to which it spans the range of relevant risks (Chart 2). Importantly, these weights should not be interpreted as probabilities that the scenarios will materialise. Rather, they indicate how relevant each scenario is for representing the risks contained in the reference measure, given the other scenarios included. Chart 2Scenario synthesis: from scenarios to a synthetic distributionSource: ECB staff illustration based on Adrian et al. (2026).Notes: The figure illustrates the conceptual steps: baseline and scenario distributions are combined to approximate a reference distribution. Weights measure scenario relevance for matching the reference distribution.ApplicationsThe ECB mainly uses the framework in three complementary ways. First, it helps us assess the relative relevance of scenarios against different measures of risk.Second, it allows us to track how scenario relevance evolves over time. For risk measures that update frequently, such as market-based measures, we can see whether a given scenario becomes more or less relevant as events unfold. Third, it provides a way to assess whether the scenarios considered cover a sufficiently broad range of risks and to identify possible gaps. Below, we illustrate each of the applications listed above. In all three examples, the distributions around the scenario paths are constructed using the ECB-BASE model.[4] ECB-BASE is the ECB’s semi-structural model for the euro area and has been the workhorse model for many scenarios. The distributions around the scenarios are derived using stochastic simulations based on draws from historical model residuals. See Angelini, E., Bokan, N., Christoffel, K., Ciccarelli, M. and Zimic, S. (2019), “Introducing ECB-BASE: The blueprint of the new ECB semi-structural model for the euro area”, Working Paper Series, No 2315, ECB, Frankfurt am Main, September. Linking Middle East conflict scenarios with different reference risk measures To illustrate the first application, we examine the milder, adverse and severe alternative scenarios for the economic impact of the Middle East conflict in the June 2026 Eurosystem staff projections. We focus on euro area inflation and evaluate the scenarios against the risk assessments from financial markets and the Survey of Professional Forecasters (SPF).[5] Another approach to computing reference distributions, which we do not consider here, relies on statistical models to estimate the predictive distribution of macroeconomic indicators, known as Macro at Risk, developed over the last decade following Adrian, T., Boyarchenko, N. and Giannone, D. (2019), "Vulnerable Growth", American Economic Review 109 (4): 1263–89. Such a measure is used by Adrian, T. et al, op. cit. For a survey of its use in the Eurosystem, see Expert Group on Macro-at-Risk Time-Series Workstream (2026), “Macro-at-Risk in the euro area” Occasional Paper Series, No 396, ECB, August. Panel a of Chart 3 compares the reference risk measures with the baseline uncertainty based on historical model residuals. The market-based measure is more dispersed, with substantially more probability mass at higher inflation rates. By contrast, the SPF’s measure is close to the baseline, although somewhat narrower and with its peak at a slightly lower inflation rate. This highlights the different risk assessments reflected in market pricing and in professional forecasters’ views. Panel b shows how the scenarios feature in each assessment: professional forecasters remain closest to the baseline. Meanwhile, financial markets place more weight on the adverse and severe scenarios. Chart 3Baseline uncertainty, risk measures and scenario synthesis weights(Panel a - y-axis: value of probability density function; Panel b - y-axis: value of scenario weight)a) Reference distributions, baseline, and scenariosb) Scenario synthesis weightsSources: Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area, June 2026; ECB Survey of Professional Forecasters (SPF), Q2 2026; Bloomberg and ECB staff calculations.Notes: Panel a compares the June 2026 baseline (red line) with selected reference distributions for HICP inflation in the first quarter of 2027. The projection cut-off date is 27 May 2026. The market-based distribution is obtained by fitting a skew-t distribution to the percentiles of the risk-neutral inflation distribution, following Garcia et al. (2026)[6] Garcia, J.A., Gimeno, R., Hinds, P., Su, H., Tretyakov, M.T. (2026), “Understanding inflation: insights from the term structure of inflation risks”, Working Paper Series, No 3294, ECB, Frankfurt am Main, October. . The estimates are based on data as of 11 June 2026 (June Governing Council meeting). The SPF distribution is from the Q2 2026 survey. Panel b shows the scenario synthesis weights for the market-based and SPF reference distributions. The weights indicate each scenario’s relevance for matching a given reference distribution.Tracking evolving market-based risk perceptionsScenario synthesis helps us understand how risk perceptions change as new information becomes available. We examine market-based risk measures for euro area inflation on 11 June, 30 June and 23 July (Chart 4). Panel a shows that, by 30 June, around the announcement of a ceasefire in the Middle East, markets saw lower inflation risks than on 11 June, although uncertainty remained. By 23 July, however, renewed regional tensions heightened energy supply concerns. Consequently, market-based inflation risks rose again. Panel b shows how the scenarios’ relative relevance changed: on 11 June the baseline mattered most, while the milder scenario became more relevant by 30 June as the balance of risks shifted in a more favourable direction. By 23 July, the geopolitical conflict had intensified further such that the adverse scenario was seen by the markets as most relevant. Overall, the chart shows how the scenario set spanned varying risk perceptions, with the relative relevance of individual scenarios adjusting to reflect new information.Chart 4Shifts in market risk perceptions surrounding the Middle East conflict(Panel a - y-axis: value of probability density function; Panel b - y-axis: value of scenario weight)a) Reference distributionsb) Scenario synthesis weightsSources: Bloomberg and ECB staff calculations.Notes: Panel a compares market-based reference distributions for euro area HICP inflation in the first quarter of 2027 on three dates: 11 June 2026 (June Governing Council meeting), 30 June 2026 (after the Memorandum of Understanding was agreed between the United States and Iran on 26 June 2026) and 23 July 2026 (July Governing Council meeting). Market-based distributions are obtained by fitting a skew-t distribution to the percentiles of the risk-neutral inflation distribution, following Garcia et al. (2026). Panel b shows the corresponding scenario-synthesis weights. Assessing scenario set coverage of market-based risksA final use of the framework is to assess how well the scenarios capture the risks reflected in a reference measure. We take the market-based measure as an example. Chart 5 compares market-based distributions with the corresponding synthetic distributions on 11 June and 30 June. The market-based distribution shifts between the two dates, reflecting a change in risk perceptions around the signing of the memorandum of understanding. Despite this shift, the synthetic distributions capture the market-implied risks reasonably well at both dates. This suggests that the scenario set spans the relevant range of risks even if perceptions change.Chart 5Scenario set coverage(y-axis: value of probability density function; x-axis: annual percentage change)a) 11 June 2026b) 30 June 2026Source: ECB staff calculations.Notes: The chart compares market-based reference distributions with their corresponding synthetic distributions for euro area HICP inflation in the first quarter of 2027. The market-data vintages are 11 June 2026 (June Governing Council meeting) in Panel a, and 30 June 2026 (after the Memorandum of Understanding agreed between the United States and Iran on 26 June 2026) in Panel b.ConclusionScenario synthesis does not replace expert judgement. Judgement remains essential when selecting and designing scenarios, constructing scenario distributions and choosing the appropriate reference risk distribution. What scenario synthesis does provide is a transparent framework connecting these elements. The key policy question is whether the scenarios we construct cover the risks that policymakers, markets or forecasters currently see. By combining baseline uncertainty, scenario narratives and reference risk measures, scenario synthesis offers a structured way to monitor shifts in risk perceptions, assess scenario coverage and, finally, communicate uncertainty around the macroeconomic outlook.The views expressed in each blog entry are those of the author(s) and do not necessarily represent the views of the European Central Bank and the Eurosystem.Check out The ECB Blog and subscribe for future posts.For topics relating to banking supervision, why not have a look at The Supervision Blog?null See Ciccarelli, M., Darracq Pariès, P., Landau, B. and Sousa, J.
